intro: Willistown Township, in Chester County west of Philadelphia, is rolling farm and woodland cut by Crum Creek, with quiet suburban streets on its edge by Malvern. Readers have sent us two big trees here: an American sycamore about 6.5 metres round by the old stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses the creek, and a white oak on Bryan Avenue whose crown fills half a front lawn. Both stand on private ground, so look from the road.
meta_description: Two big trees readers sent from Willistown, Pennsylvania: a sycamore by the Crum Creek bridge and a wide white oak on Bryan Avenue.

trees.name: The Sycamore at the Crum Creek Bridge

location.address: Beside White Horse Road at its bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA

trees.story:
A reader put a tape round this sycamore and got about 6.5 metres. That is a big trunk for any tree in Pennsylvania, and the American sycamore is counted among the largest broadleaf trees of the eastern United States. They like exactly this kind of place, a creek bank with water close to the roots.

The reader who sent it called it "so massive and robust" and placed it "near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, closer to Paoli, not very near Media". Their pin lands on the spot where White Horse Road crosses the creek. Nobody we have read has written about this tree, so we do not know its age, who planted it, or whether it was planted at all. A sycamore this broad by a creek is often a seedling that simply found good ground.

Their photographs, taken in autumn sun, show the pale upper limbs that give the species away, the mottled grey bark lower down, and a base that flares out over a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence. If you go, look from the road side and leave the fences alone; we do not know who owns the ground it grows on. If you know its history, or have measured it yourself, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad sycamore with pale, almost white upper limbs and mottled grey bark, its base flaring over a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence, by the stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses Crum Creek.
verified_sources: A reader's photographs and note through the app, 2026-11-15, with a pin they placed by hand at the White Horse Road bridge over Crum Creek
trees.verify_notes: 2026-11-15: sent by a reader through the app with two photographs (whole tree in autumn colour, trunk base), girth 650 cm by their measure, note: near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, closer to Paoli, not very near Media. Pin placed by hand, no GPS fix; it reverse-geocodes (Nominatim) exactly onto the White Horse Road bridge over Crum Creek (OSM way 74635054, bridge=yes), which matches the note; a stone wall at the right edge of the first photograph fits a bridge parapet. No written source found (searches for the bridge, the township, the Willistown Conservation Trust; not in the Pennsylvania champion lists we hold). Species from the photographs: pale upper limbs, plane-type bark and leaves; the reader also named it American sycamore. Ownership of the ground not known; access line tells visitors to look from the road. Published on Hidde's rule that a stranger's good photograph of a tree worth the walk is not held for a written source; precision approximate because the pin was placed by hand. Not the Tyler Arboretum trees in media-pennsylvania (about 9.6 km south-east).
trees.access: Free to see from White Horse Road by the bridge, by the reader's account. Ownership of the ground is not known, so stay on the road side and do not cross fences; take care with traffic.

trees.name: The White Oak of Bryan Avenue
trees.age_estimate: more than 300 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Bryan Avenue, Duffryn Mawr, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA 19355

trees.story:
"The spread of this oak is half the front lawn of this house," wrote the reader who sent it to us from Bryan Avenue, a quiet residential street in the Duffryn Mawr corner of Willistown Township, Chester County.

Their photographs bear that out. The trunk is short and massive, its pale grey bark broken into long shallow plates and swollen with burrs, and only a few metres up it splits into a crown of thick, crooked limbs. They run out almost level over the grass, one of them reaching past the roof of the low house behind, and with most of the leaves down in November you can follow every bend of them against the sky. The last leaves hang on in rusty red, the way a white oak holds its foliage late into autumn.

The reader puts it at more than 300 years old and its girth at about 510 centimetres. Those figures are theirs; we have found nothing written about this tree. If they are right, the oak was growing here long before the street was laid out around it. If you know its history, or the story the neighbours tell about it, tell us.

It stands on a private front lawn. Look at it from the street, and leave the garden to the people who live there.
trees.how_to_recognise: A huge, low-branched oak alone on a front lawn on Bryan Avenue: a short pale trunk with burrs on it, splitting a few metres up into thick crooked limbs that reach out over the grass and past the roof of the low grey house behind.
verified_sources: A reader's three photographs and note through the app, 2026-11-20, with a pin they placed by hand on Bryan Avenue, Willistown Township
trees.access: Seen from Bryan Avenue. The lawn it stands on is a private front garden, so stay on the street.

pin_source.note: The reader placed this pin on the map in the app; not a GPS fix. It reverse-geocodes (Nominatim) onto Bryan Avenue, Duffryn Mawr, which the street in the photographs fits.

trees.verify_notes: 2026-11-20 reader judge: sent by a reader through the app (69cf3021-612b-4af4-a051-e91406fac8ca), three photographs viewed: the whole oak from the street side in late-autumn sun, a short pale trunk under a huge crown of crooked limbs reaching over a front lawn and past a low house roof, rusty last leaves, daylight, colour; two more frames from the lawn edge show the trunk with its burrs and the limbs spreading level from it. The reader's own figures: name 'White Oak in Willistown', species 'White Oak', age '300+', girth 510 cm; note: 'The spread of this oak is half the front lawn of this house.'. Species from the photographs: lobed oak leaves held late in rusty red, pale platy bark: white oak, as the reader named it. On a private front lawn but in plain view from the street (the photographs are taken from the street side), so it ships with an access line to stay on the street (Hidde 2026-11-17, 'not public is also not 100% dismiss if its viewable'). Published under the closed list for a reader's tree; approximate because the pin was placed by hand. Second tree of Willistown; same reader as wtn_001. 2026-11-20 reader judge: the reader wrote back (feedback 1332) that the neighbour who owns the lawn is happy for the tree to be on the site and knows it may bring visitors; the access line stays as it is (look from the street).

question_meta: The biggest trees readers have found in Willistown, PA: a sycamore by the Crum Creek bridge and a white oak on Bryan Avenue, and how to see them.
question_answer: Readers have sent us two big trees in Willistown Township, Chester County. An American sycamore stands by the old stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses Crum Creek, about 650 cm round by a reader's measure. A white oak on Bryan Avenue in Duffryn Mawr is about 510 cm round and more than 300 years old by a reader's estimate. No age has been published for either. See both from the road.
question_context: Both trees came to us from a reader through the app in November 2026, with photographs and their own measurements. The sycamore grows near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, closer to Paoli than to Media, its base on a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence; their photographs show the pale upper limbs and mottled grey bark of the species, which is counted among the largest broadleaf trees of the eastern United States and favours creek banks like this one. The white oak is about four kilometres north-west, on a front lawn on Bryan Avenue, a residential street in the Duffryn Mawr corner of the township near Malvern. Its crooked limbs spread over half the lawn, and the reader puts it at more than 300 years old. We have found nothing written about either tree, so their figures are the only ones. Both stand on private ground: look from the road and leave fences and gardens alone.

faq.a: The sycamore is about 650 cm round and the white oak about 510 cm, both by the measure of the reader who sent them. Nobody else has published a figure.
The reader puts the white oak at more than 300 years. Nobody has published an age for either tree. If you know their history, tell us.

The sycamore is beside White Horse Road at its stone bridge over Crum Creek; the white oak is on a front lawn on Bryan Avenue in Duffryn Mawr. Both pins are approximate, and both trees are seen from the road.
